Am I required to carry it?

Only if your home is in a high-risk zone (A or V) and your mortgage is from a federally regulated lender, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Check your zone on FEMA's flood map.

72.8% of Illinois's NFIP policies are in high-risk zones (not 72.8% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Buy it now: most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there's no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). NFIP covers up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents, which is a separate policy. To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. Past aid paid here is in “Did the government pay homeowners after floods?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Why do sites quote different averages for Illinois?

Because they measure different things. From the same FEMA records, the typical single-family home pays $1,128 a year, but the average across every policy type is $1,688.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Median cost, single-family homes$1,128premium plus fees; the middle policy
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$1,300pulled up by a few expensive policies
Median premium only, single-family homes$895before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Average premium only, single-family homes$1,040the figure many sites quote
Median cost, every policy type$1,202adds condos, rentals and businesses
Average cost, every policy type$1,688

Published averages rarely say which of these they are, or which year. All six here come from the NFIP policies in force on July 31, 2026.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

39.2% of bills here can keep rising: they pay less than FEMA's full-risk price. Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. Median premium $895, full-risk $1,026 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$895
  • Median full-risk premium$1,026
  • Pay below full-risk39.2% of 17,497

Years to the full-risk price: By law most premiums cannot rise more than 18% a year (FloodSmart puts it at 18–25% for most policyholders); the cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. At the 18% cap, a policy at today's median premium ($895) would take at least about 1 annual renewal to reach the median full-risk premium ($1,026). This is the limit on how fast a bill can climb, not a forecast of any one policy.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 52,890 NFIP flood claims and $579.8 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2008, 2013 and 1993.

Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2008 ($104,835,282), 2013 ($93,078,418), 1993 ($67,392,622). Total paid $579,842,974: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 52,890 claims since 1978 against 30,962 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

NFIP covers up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents, which is a separate policy. Rebuilding cost is the replacement-cost figure on each single-family primary-home policy record.

How often do the same homes flood here?

Some homes here flood again and again: 190,529 flood-damage applications in FEMA's disaster-aid records came from homes that flooded more than once; 33,098 of those records came from homes hit in four or more.

  • Repeat-flood damage records190,529
  • Records from homes hit 4+ times33,098

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so this counts damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid applications since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Repetitive-Loss Flood Properties. Data effective October 26, 2026; retrieved October 26, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Did the government pay homeowners after floods?

Yes, but not much per household: FEMA approved $982.0 million for homeowners here, about $2,915 per registration, against an average paid flood claim of $14,411.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance.

Reconciliation & data completeness

Our record counts match the API's own totals; FEMA's official policy count is not yet joined for Illinois.

In-force count: 30,962 policy units (from 24,012 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 24012/24012 fetched; claims: 52890/52890 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why any one premium changes — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
